title: Lakshmana's rage and restraint
hook: only the weak blame fate, Lakshmana says, and then he has to decide what to do with his strength
carry: the rage stays, he doesn't spend it

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's rage and restraint, part one, the rage. Rama has done nothing wrong, he said, and I'll fight for him. Did you find the love underneath an anger? Today, the argument and the restraint. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

A few days ago, Rama told Lakshmana not to blame Kaikeyi, because what had happened was daiva, something larger than any one person. It's a gentle idea. Lakshmana hates it. He's standing with his brow knotted, and Valmiki says he's breathing hard, like an angry snake in its hole. And he answers his brother with an argument that people have been quoting ever since. It's the other side of the old question: how much is fate, and how much is up to us?
screen: `DAIVA, RAMA SAID.` → `LAKSHMANA HATES IT.` → `HOW MUCH IS UP TO US?`

segments.voice: Here is Lakshmana's case. Fate, he says, is what weak people talk about. The brave and strong don't sit waiting for it. A real hero pushes fate aside with his own effort. If you call this fate, you're giving up before you've even tried. Then he holds up his arms. These aren't for decoration, he says. They're for protecting you. Today the people will see which is stronger, fate or me. Let me take the kingdom for you, and you rule it. It's a powerful speech, and Valmiki doesn't make it foolish. In Hindu thought, effort, purushakara, is honored just as seriously as fate. Plenty of teachers would side with Lakshmana's view on another day. But listen to what Rama does. He doesn't argue the philosophy again. He wipes away Lakshmana's tears, and speaks to him as a brother. Know that I am determined to keep our father's word, he says. Stand with me in this. That's the whole answer. And Lakshmana listens. The text describes him with his head lowered, still grieving, still angry, and silent. This is the restraint in his name today. He doesn't stop feeling the rage. He chooses not to spend it. He has the arms, the bow, the courage, and probably the soldiers. What he gives his brother is the thing that's hardest for a strong person to give: holding back. And immediately, the energy has somewhere to go. If you're going to the forest, Lakshmana says, then so am I.
screen: `ONLY THE WEAK TALK OF FATE.` · `THESE ARMS ARE FOR YOU.` · `RAMA WIPES AWAY HIS TEARS.` · `THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.` · then, large: `THEN SO AM I.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the body be heavy. Close your hands into loose fists, and feel your own strength in them. Hold them like that for a few breaths. Then, slowly, open them, palms up, resting on your knees. Notice that the strength is still there in the open hands. Breathe with them open. Holding back isn't the same as being weak. The bell holds the time.
Purushakara, human effort, the old partner and rival of fate. Lakshmana argues that heroes push fate aside, then lowers his head, keeps his strength unspent, and chooses to go with Rama.
Your line: the rage stays, he doesn't spend it. Today, when you could win by force, try opening your hands instead. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often set Rama's speech on daiva, fate, beside Lakshmana's speech on purushakara, human effort, and leave listeners to weigh both.

match.prompt: fate or effort — tap the pairs.
pairs: only the weak talk of fate

myth: Valmiki makes Lakshmana's argument look foolish
he gives it full force; effort is honored in Hindu thought too.
Rama answers by debating fate again
he wipes Lakshmana's tears and asks him to stand with him.
Lakshmana ends by deciding to go to the forest
if you're going, he says, so am I.

fork.setup: you're Lakshmana. you have the strength to take the throne for your brother, and he's asked you to stand with him instead. what do you do?
options: take it anyway; he'll thank you later.
lower your head, hold back, and go with him.
go home and stay out of it.
fork.reveal: he falls silent, still grieving and angry, and turns his strength to following Rama into exile.

original.note: Sanskrit puruṣakāra: human effort, what a person does; the old partner and rival of daiva, fate.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lakshmana gives up his anger.
what it means: he keeps the anger but chooses not to spend it, and turns it into following Rama.
what a scholar hears: Lakshmana's speech against fate is the counterweight to Rama's speech on daiva, and Valmiki lets both stand without declaring a winner.
recall: young king, the heir who shares the rule
